raw_text:
For decades, implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (ICDs) have served as a cornerstone in the primary and secondary prevention of sudden cardiac death (SCD) [1,2]. However, conventional transvenous ICD (TV-ICD) systems are associated with significant long-term, lead-related morbidity. These complications include lead fracture, insulation failure, venous occlusion, tricuspid valve damage, and systemic endocarditis [3-5]. To overcome these intravascular lead-related challenges, the subcutaneous ICD (S-ICD) was developed, placing the entire system in an extrathoracic position [6]. 

Early clinical experience with the S-ICD was validated through prospective trials, including the S-ICD Investigational Device Exemption (IDE) study, which demonstrated high conversion rates for induced ventricular fibrillation [7]. This was followed by a pooled analysis of the IDE study and the EFFORTLESS registry, confirming the clinical utility of the device in a larger, more diverse patient cohort [8,9]. Real-world registries further demonstrated that S-ICD implantation results in durable protection over mid-term follow-up [10]. More recently, the long-term results of the EFFORTLESS study showed that the S-ICD remains highly reliable over five years, with low rates of device-related complications and system infections [11].

The evidence comparing S-ICDs to TV-ICDs was significantly bolstered by the landmark PRAETORIAN trial [12]. PRAETORIAN was the first randomized controlled trial to establish the non-inferiority of S-ICDs against TV-ICDs regarding a composite endpoint of inappropriate shocks and device-related complications. A subsequent secondary analysis of the PRAETORIAN cohort clarified that although S-ICD recipients had a higher incidence of inappropriate shocks, they experienced a significant reduction in lead-related complications and systemic infections compared to TV-ICD recipients [13]. 

To optimize S-ICD performance in typical, primary prevention cohorts with low ejection fractions, the UNTOUCHED trial investigated contemporary S-ICD programming (employing high-rate conditional therapy zones and modern discrimination algorithms). UNTOUCHED achieved a very low inappropriate shock rate of 3.1% at one year [14]. Concurrently, the randomized ATLAS trial proved that S-ICD implantation dramatically reduces major perioperative lead-related complications by 92% compared to TV-ICD implantation, highlighting the acute safety benefits of an entirely subcutaneous system [15]. These findings are supported by the five-year results of the S-ICD System Post-Approval Study (PAS), which confirmed low overall complication rates [16] and highly predictable clinical profiles, with infections mostly restricted to the early post-operative period [17].

Despite these improvements, inappropriate shocks remain a key clinical challenge, primarily arising from cardiac or extracardiac oversensing [18]. T-wave oversensing represents a major cause of inappropriate delivery of therapy, which can often be predicted or managed with exercise-optimized template screening and reprogramming [19]. To mitigate this issue, advanced signal filtering software has been introduced. Prospective blinded evaluations of the SMART Pass high-pass filter have demonstrated that enabling this algorithm reduces inappropriate shocks by up to 68% without compromising the detection or conversion of true ventricular tachyarrhythmias [20]. This is supported by earlier morphological discrimination templates [21] and standardized software algorithms [22] that improve specificity against supraventricular tachycardias.

The surgical technique for S-ICD implantation has also evolved significantly. The original three-incision approach has been largely superseded by the two-incision technique, which avoids the superior parasternal incision, thereby improving cosmetic outcomes and reducing the potential risk of lead tip erosion or local infection [23]. Furthermore, operators have transitioned from placing the pulse generator in a subcutaneous pocket to creating an intermuscular pocket between the serratus anterior and latissimus dorsi muscles [24,25]. This intermuscular approach reduces post-operative pain, decreases generator visibility, and lowers the risk of pocket erosion, particularly in patients with a low body mass index.

The chief limitation of S-ICD therapy remains its inability to deliver long-term bradycardia pacing, cardiac resynchronization, or anti-tachycardia pacing (ATP) [26]. Early feasibility studies demonstrated that a leadless pacemaker could be safely co-implanted with an S-ICD without causing electrical interference or oversensing [26,27]. This synergy paved the way for modular cardiac rhythm management (mCRM) systems. In 2024, the primary results of the MODULAR ATP trial were published, confirming that a modular, wirelessly communicating leadless pacemaker-defibrillator system is safe and highly effective at delivering ATP to painlessly terminate monomorphic ventricular tachycardia [28]. 

In conclusion, clinical evidence, including propensity score-matched analyses [29] and early head-to-head algorithm comparisons [30], has established the S-ICD as a mature and highly effective therapy. It provides robust protection against sudden cardiac death while avoiding the long-term hazards of transvenous leads. The integration of modular leadless pacing systems represents a paradigm shift that will likely expand S-ICD eligibility to a wider spectrum of patients in the coming years.
